clinicalPearls: The most common functional ovarian cyst, formed when a dominant follicle fails to rupture at ovulation and continues to enlarge
Usually a thin-walled, unilocular, anechoic simple cyst on ultrasound, without solid components or internal vascularity
Frequently asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, though larger cysts can cause a dull unilateral ache or pressure
The great majority resolve spontaneously over one or more menstrual cycles, so a short-interval follow-up scan often confirms the diagnosis
Simple cysts in premenopausal women are almost always benign and can be managed expectantly
Complications include rupture, causing transient sharp pain and sometimes a small amount of free fluid, and, in larger cysts, torsion
Persistent or enlarging cysts, or those with atypical features, warrant reassessment and consideration of an alternative diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: During a normal cycle a dominant follicle matures and ruptures to release the oocyte. If ovulation does not occur, or if the follicle fails to involute afterwards, it continues to secrete fluid and enlarges into a simple cyst lined by granulosa and theca cells. Because the cyst arises from the normal cyclical activity of the ovary, it is termed functional and typically regresses as the hormonal milieu changes across subsequent cycles.
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound characterising the cyst as simple and unilocular
Interval follow-up ultrasound to confirm spontaneous resolution
Pregnancy test to help interpret ovarian findings
Tumour markers where the appearance is atypical or the woman is postmenopausal
Structured risk assessment of the adnexal mass when malignancy cannot be excluded
redFlags: Solid components, thick septations, or internal vascularity suggesting neoplasia
A simple cyst arising in a postmenopausal woman that requires closer evaluation
Acute severe pain suggesting torsion of a larger cyst
Rupture with significant pain or free fluid
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent; most follicular cysts resolve spontaneously without intervention and rarely cause lasting problems.
pitfalls: Over-investigating or over-treating small simple cysts that would resolve on their own
Failing to consider torsion when a larger cyst causes acute pain
Applying premenopausal reassurance inappropriately to a postmenopausal woman
Assuming persistence equates to malignancy without structured reassessment
